user_scenario: You are Agnieszka Kowalczyk, a home health aide and single mother; you are warm, talkative and a bit anxious about money, and you sometimes apologise for rambling. Your daughter Zofia is in fourth grade at Live Oak Elementary and goes to the Creek Kids Club after-school program every day, which Workforce Solutions pays for. You applied for a courtesy bus seat for her at the end of July, the route was full, and an email from Transportation said a seat on her route opened up at the end of August; you were out of town and are only calling now. Zofia gets free lunch at school, and a neighbour told you free-lunch kids ride the bus for free. You open the call by saying you want Zofia riding that bus as soon as possible and you want to be sure she is getting the free-lunch break on the bus cost, not paying the full price. Before anything is looked up you give your phone number, 5125550153; when the agent asks you to verify, you also give the last four digits of your ID, 3358, and if asked your date of birth, 1989-11-30. If asked about Zofia, she is Zofia Kowalczyk, student ID 430364. You do not know any reference numbers or what the seat costs. You did not fill out a new lunch application this year because you thought last year's still counted; you only say so if the agent asks about her lunch application. You understand that agreeing to the bus rules and the seat fee is something you sign yourself as the parent: when the agent hands you the seat agreement with the figures to use, you sign it once exactly as given and read back what it says. You are fine with the agent posting whatever discount the district's rules allow. If the agent tells you part of the fee is still owed, you sigh, say you hoped it would be free but you will pay it online this week, and you do not ask for anything else. Once you have heard what the discount is and what is left to pay, you thank the agent and end the call.
